title: Bagan
hookLine: thousands of temples on the plain of Bagan in Myanmar

lines: TEMPLES AS FAR AS THE EYE CAN SEE.
cards: Dawn, on a wide dry plain beside the Irrawaddy River in Myanmar.
As the mist thins, shapes rise out of it: temples and stupas of red brick and white plaster, some enormous, some no bigger than a garden shed, scattered as far as the eye can reach.
The plain is quiet, except for a bell somewhere, a broom on a step, a few early visitors taking off their sandals at a doorway.
The donors who paid for these buildings called them gifts, and some carved their wishes in stone.

teach.h: A KING, A MONK, A WAR.
teach.b: First, the king and the monk. The Burmese chronicles tell how King Anawrahta of Bagan met a monk named Shin Arahan, who taught him the Theravada teaching.
They say the king wanted the scriptures and monks of Thaton, a kingdom to the south, and when its king refused him, he went to war and brought them back.

Historians question parts of that story, but it is how the tradition remembers Bagan's beginning. Second, building as giving. Over generations, kings, queens, officials and ordinary families built on the plain.
In Buddhist teaching, generous giving makes merit, good that ripens in this life and in lives to come, and a temple was a great gift to make.
Inscriptions left by donors survive, and some record their wishes: to meet a future Buddha, to reach nibbana, to share the merit with their parents and with all beings. Third, the inside.
Some temples are not solid mounds at all.
You can walk into them, through dim corridors painted with scenes from the Buddha's past lives, past rows of seated Buddhas lit by small windows. Fourth, the plain today.
Earthquakes have shaken Bagan, and some temples have cracked, fallen or been rebuilt. It is still a place of devotion: people make offerings, light candles and walk barefoot through the corridors.
A plain of temples is what happens when people, over a long time, each decide to give something that will outlast them.

how: Buddhists in Myanmar visit the temples of Bagan to offer flowers, candles and food, walk barefoot through the shrines, and dedicate the merit of their giving to their families and to all beings.

games.q: you're a family in Bagan with a little saved. what do you do with it?
o: build a small shrine, and share the merit.
games.why: donors of many ranks built on the plain, and their inscriptions share the merit with parents and with all beings.

practice: See the plain at dawn, mist over flat dry ground and temples rising near and far, and choose one small temple, built perhaps not by a king but by a family putting what they could spare into bricks.
On each out-breath, let a good wish go out from you, as the donors did, toward someone you love, or toward everyone.

wordCard.voice: Bagan. The plain beside the Irrawaddy in Myanmar, where kings and ordinary families built temples and stupas, gift after gift. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: puñña, merit, the good that generous giving makes.

carryVoice: Your line: a plain of temples. Gift after gift, it became a landscape. Day eight hundred eighty-five, done.
